Five echoes from Week 9

1. “Okay lah, we'll order 2 kopi”: what did the normalizer do to “2” before scoring?

rewrote it as “two” on both sides, so a correct transcript went from 100% WER to 0%

2. What can one overall WER hide?

a gap between groups: report WER for each group, with utterance and word counts

3. Forced alignment is Viterbi with what already known?

the words: Viterbi decides only when each phone starts and ends

4. What does a forced alignment give every phone?

a start and an end time, so a duration

5. What happens to a word missing from the aligner's dictionary, like “makan”?

it gets no phones (MFA labels it spn, spoken noise); the fix is one dictionary line

Recognition and synthesis, side by side

Recognition and synthesis are inverses

  • Recognition keeps only the words; pitch, timing and voice are discarded
  • Synthesis must supply them: “2 kopi” fixes the words, not the pitch, timing or voice
  • The text underspecifies the speech: many waveforms fit one sentence
The classical pipeline

The front end: from raw text to a plan

raw text“Dr Tan paid $2.50”
→
normalizeexpand numbers, symbols
→
G2Pwords → phones
→
prosodypitch, duration, stress
→
specificationphones, durations, F0
→
back endmake the wave
  • The front end is linguistics before acoustics: phonology, morphology and syntax decide the plan
  • The back end only renders the plan
  • Each arrow can fail on its own
  • A front-end error is never repaired later: if G2P gives the wrong phone, the back end pronounces the wrong phone clearly

This is the classical pipeline. Neural models (Week 11) learn some of these steps inside the network, but most still normalize text first.

The heart of the front end

Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P): from letters to phones

  • English orthography hides the sounds: “through”, “though”, “tough” share letters, not phones
  • Dictionary first (CMUdict); letter-to-sound rules or a trained model for words not in it (out-of-vocabulary, OOV)
  • Heteronyms (one spelling, two pronunciations) need the sentence: “a record” vs “to record” is a part-of-speech decision; “I read it yesterday” vs “I will read it” needs the tense
When a word is not in the dictionary
  • G2P falls back on letter-to-sound rules: written by hand (as in eSpeak NG) or learned from a dictionary such as CMUdict
  • eSpeak NG (US English) reads makan as /ˈmækən/, kopi as /ˈkoʊpi/, Tampines as /ˈtæmpaɪnz/
  • The same gap as Week 9, where MFA turned a missing word into spn
One spelling, two pronunciations

the desert / to desert
ˈdɛzərt   dɪˈzɜrt

record (noun) / record (verb)
ˈrɛkərd   rɪˈkɔrd

stress and vowels flip with the syntax

Build the output from rules

Formant synthesis, in one line

Formant synthesis is
source-filter theory, run as a generator.

Week 3: a vowel is a source shaped by a filter.
Here: choose the source, set the formants by hand, and a vowel comes out.

Formant synthesis, from the 1950s

Formant synthesis: draw the resonances

  • Source: a buzz at F0 with all its harmonics (voiced), or noise (voiceless)
  • Filter: resonators at F1, F2 and F3; their frequencies set the vowel
  • No recordings at all: the voice is a handful of numbers over time, drawn by a phonetician
  • The Klatt synthesizer (1980; revised 1990), in Praat as the KlattGrid: you try it at the end of this section
  • Fully controllable; clearly robotic
Why linguists use it: stimuli for perception experiments
hear step:
  • One cue at a time: only the start of F2 moves, in equal steps (illustrative values)
  • Listeners' “ba or da?” answers switch suddenly between two steps: categorical perception (Liberman et al. 1957)
  • Like Week 2's Ganong continuum: where does /ba/ become /da/?
Worked example: one buzz, three vowels

Sweep the formants, hear the vowel change

  • The gray comb is the source: F0 harmonics, unchanging
  • The coral curve is the filter: peaks at F1, F2, F3
  • The teal comb is the output: harmonics shaped by the filter, the spectrum you hear

Only the filter changes; the source is the same for Week 1's /i/, /ɑ/ and /u/. The sound: Praat's KlattGrid making the same sweep.

Formant synthesis

Formant synthesis: strengths and weaknesses

Strengths
  • Full control of every parameter
  • Small: kilobytes, no stored audio
  • Any sound, human or not
  • Every parameter has a phonetic meaning
Weaknesses
  • Sounds robotic: a small rule set misses the detail of real voices
  • Each language and voice is tuned by hand
  • Natural prosody is very hard to write as rules
A VOICE KEPT FOR LIFE
  • Stephen Hawking kept his 1980s formant voice until his death in 2018: it had become part of his identity
  • Formant speech is highly intelligible, even when it is not natural

Built from numbers.
Next: built from recordings.

After the break: concatenative synthesis, which joins pieces of recorded speech, then articulatory synthesis.

The opposite philosophy

Why synthesize sound you could just replay?

  • Record one speaker for hours, cut the audio into small units, and join them into new sentences
  • Every unit is real human speech; the difficulty is the joins
  • The standard unit: the diphone, from the middle of one phone to the middle of the next
WHY DIPHONES, NOT PHONES
  • Coarticulation (Week 3): each phone's edges change with its neighbors
  • Phone middles are the most stable part, so diphones are cut there
  • Each transition stays inside one recorded unit, never at a join
Concatenative synthesis: a short history

From a talking clock to unit selection

1933
A talking clock
Paris: words recorded on photographic strips, played in order
1953
One piece per phoneme
Harris (Columbia): mostly unintelligible, because coarticulation is lost
1958
The diphone
Peterson, Wang & Sivertsen (Michigan): cut at phone middles, the most stable part
1967–77
Diphones as numbers
Stored as synthesizer settings, not audio: IBM, then Bell Labs
1990demo in Praat
PSOLA
CNET, France: change a recording’s pitch and duration
1996★ hardest idea
Unit selection
Hunt & Black (ATR, Japan): thousands of candidates, chosen by target and join cost
2001
Unit selection goes commercial
AT&T Natural Voices; Siri still used a hybrid in 2017
2016Week 11
WaveNet
A neural network beats splicing in listening tests

Sources: Abgrall et al. (2013); Harris (1953); Peterson, Wang & Sivertsen (1958); Dixon & Maxey (1968); Olive (1977); Klatt (1987); Moulines & Charpentier (1990); Hunt & Black (1996); Burdick (2003); Capes et al. (2017); van den Oord et al. (2016).

Changing the prosody of a recording · Moulines & Charpentier (1990)

PSOLA: new pitch, same vowel

  • A diphone keeps the speaker’s pitch and timing; the plan asks for others
  • Cut the wave into overlapping pieces, one per pitch pulse
  • Pieces closer together: higher pitch. Repeat or drop pieces: longer or shorter
  • Each piece keeps its shape, so the formants and the vowel stay (nearly) the same, if the change is moderate
How it works: one synthetic vowel, five steps

★ The hardest idea this week

Unit selection: the cheapest path
through real recordings.

Target cost: does this recording fit the plan? Join cost: does it join smoothly to its neighbor?
Viterbi finds the sequence with the lowest total.

Concatenative synthesis, scaled up (Hunt & Black 1996)

Unit selection: a huge library, one best path

  • Not one recording per unit but thousands, spoken in every context
  • Two costs to minimize: target cost (does this unit fit the plan?) and join cost (do neighboring units join smoothly?)
  • Choose the sequence of units with the lowest total cost
  • The table trick's fourth appearance: DTW kept the minimum (Week 5), Viterbi the maximum (Week 6), CTC the sum (Week 8)
  • Here Viterbi keeps the lowest total cost, and so chooses recordings
  • Lattice: one column per target diphone, one node per candidate recording
YOU HAVE HEARD THIS
  • Car navigation voices and automated phone menus of the 2000s
  • Siri's voices as late as 2017 (hybrid unit selection; Capes et al. 2017)
  • Natural when the right units exist; an audible jump when a rare word forces a poor join
Worked example (invented rules): where a target cost comes from

Target cost: compare the plan with each recording

The plan for /ɔ-p/ in “kopi”, from the front end

PENALTY RULES (INVENTED)
    IN REAL SYSTEMS
    • Many more features: neighboring phones, position in the phrase, and more
    • The weights are tuned, by hand or automatically
    • Newer systems measure the distance from what a statistical model predicts (Google, Gonzalvo et al. 2016; Siri, Capes et al. 2017)
    Worked example (illustrative costs): three diphones for “kopi”

    The lattice, and the cheapest path through it

    • Each row: one recording of “kopi”; the number in a node is its target cost: how badly it fits the plan (0 = perfect)
    • Each edge: the join cost: 0 inside one recording, otherwise 0.3
    • Total = target costs + join costs; the table fills like DTW's (Week 5) and traces back like Viterbi's (Week 6)
    V(u) = T(u) + minp [ V(p) + J(p, u) ]

    V: cheapest total from the start to u (a running total)
    u: a candidate in this column · p: one in the previous column

    Concatenative synthesis

    Concatenative synthesis: strengths and weaknesses

    Strengths
    • With the right units, close to the recorded speaker
    • No acoustic model to get wrong
    • The voice is that speaker's own voice
    Weaknesses
    • Hours of studio recording per voice
    • Gigabytes of audio
    • Audible join glitches in rare contexts
    • Only the recorded style: a calm speaker's units cannot whisper
    HYBRIDS, THEN NEURAL
    • Later systems used a statistical model to smooth the joins
    • From 2016, neural networks generated the whole waveform (WaveNet), and it sounded better than splicing
    • Week 11 tells that story
    ə
    The third approach

    Articulatory synthesis: model the vocal tract, not the sound

    • Formant synthesis models the output; concatenation reuses recordings
    • Articulatory synthesis models the vocal tract itself: tongue, lips, glottis, as a physical tube
    • Push air through the simulated tube, shape it, and sound comes out by physics, not by rules or replay
    ʃ
    Articulatory synthesis · what to try

    Play a vocal tract with your hands

    • Drag the tongue body and watch a vowel slide around the space you drew in Week 1
    • Pinch a constriction for a fricative; tap a full closure for a stop burst
    • The articulators from phonetics class, as controls you can hear
    • In class: /i/, /ɑ/, /u/, then /ʃ/, then a stop
    • Then a whole word: much harder, because every articulator must move in time
    STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES
    • Closest to how speech is produced
    • Hardest to control, slowest to run, rarely used in products
    • Lets you hear an articulatory diagram

    Three classical back ends

    The three answers, compared

    FORMANT

    Model the output

    Build the spectrum from rules. Tiny, controllable, robotic. Any sound, no data.

    CONCATENATIVE

    Reuse the recordings

    Join recorded speech fragments. Natural on common text, brittle on rare, and huge.

    ARTICULATORY

    Model the cause

    Simulate the tract. Physically realistic; slow and hard to control; rarely used in products.

    • All three predate neural synthesis; each shows one part of what a voice is made of
    • Week 11: neural models learn the voice from (text, audio) pairs: natural, but harder to control

    • A: says any new word or particle, but sounds robotic
    • B: most natural; rare words and contexts get poor joins; needs many hours of recording
    • C: still a research tool
    • Week 11: neural synthesis aims for B's naturalness with A's flexibility

    Course definitions, with sources

    This week, formally

    DEFINITION
    Grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P)

    The front-end task of mapping written words to their pronunciations, by dictionary lookup with a rule-based or statistical model for unseen words and context for heteronyms.

    Course wording. Taylor (2009), Text-to-Speech Synthesis, ch. “Pronunciation”, 192–224; lexicon: CMUdict.
    DEFINITION
    Formant synthesis

    Rule-based synthesis that generates speech from an explicit source (voicing or noise) and a set of resonators at the formant frequencies: the source-filter model, run as a generator.

    Klatt (1980), JASA 67(3), 971–995; Praat's KlattGrid implements Klatt & Klatt (1990).
    DEFINITION
    Unit selection synthesis

    Concatenative synthesis that chooses, from a large recorded database, the unit sequence minimizing a combination of target cost (fit to the specification) and join cost (splice quality), by dynamic programming.

    Hunt & Black (1996), Proc. ICASSP 1996, vol. 1, 373–376; J&M Ch 17, Historical Notes (Aug 2026 draft).
    DEFINITION
    Articulatory synthesis

    Synthesis that simulates the physical vocal tract, generating sound from a model of the articulators and airflow rather than from acoustic targets or recordings.

    J&M Ch 17, Historical Notes (Aug 2026 draft); tools: Thapen (2017), Pink Trombone; Birkholz (2013), PLoS ONE 8(4), e60603 (VocalTractLab).
    Exercises: pencils out · ~7 minutes, in pairs

    Try it: front end and back end

    EX 10.1

    Expand for speech, and give one alternative reading each: “Dr Tan lives at 21 Jln Besar, unit 03-11, and paid $4.50.” Which expansions need context the string alone does not provide?

    EX 10.2

    A dictionary lists “read” with two pronunciations. Why can G2P not choose between them by lookup alone, and what information resolves it? Name one other English heteronym.

    EX 10.3

    Two target diphones, two candidates each. Target costs: col 1 [0.2, 0.6]; col 2 [0.5, 0.3]. Join cost: 0 if both come from the same recording (i = j), otherwise 0.1. Find the minimum-total path and its cost.

    EX 10.4

    Match each approach (formant, unit selection, articulatory) to “models the output / reuses recordings / models the cause”. Which degrades most gracefully on a brand-new Singlish word in no database, and why?

    Worked answers in the appendix at the end of this deck.

    Before you go

    Four things to remember

    1. Synthesis is recognition reversed: the text leaves out pitch, timing and voice, so the synthesizer must supply them

    2. Half of classical TTS is the front end: normalization and G2P, linguistics before acoustics

    3. Three back ends: model the output, reuse recordings, model the cause

    4. Unit selection is the table trick's fourth appearance: the cheapest path of target plus join costs through a lattice of recordings

    Appendix: worked answers

    Answers

    EX 10.1

    “Dr” → Doctor (before a name), not Drive; “21” → twenty-one; “Jln” → Jalan; “03-11” → oh three, eleven (a unit number), not “three minus eleven”; “$4.50” → four dollars fifty. Context decides “Dr” and “03-11”: the token alone cannot.

    EX 10.2

    One spelling, two pronunciations, so lookup returns both. The choice needs the tense (present “read” /riːd/, past “read” /rɛd/), which comes from the surrounding words (yesterday, will), not from the word itself. Another heteronym: “lead” (verb /liːd/, the metal /lɛd/), where the part of speech decides; or “tear”, “bow”, “live”.

    EX 10.3

    Paths (col1 → col2): 1→1 = 0.2 + 0 + 0.5 = 0.7; 1→2 = 0.2 + 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.6; 2→1 = 0.6 + 0.1 + 0.5 = 1.2; 2→2 = 0.6 + 0 + 0.3 = 0.9. Minimum is 1 → 2, cost 0.6: the cheap target in column 1 is worth a small join penalty to reach the cheap target in column 2.

    EX 10.4

    Formant synthesis models the output, unit selection reuses recordings, articulatory synthesis models the cause. Most graceful on a new word: formant (or articulatory), since rules or physics need no recording of the word; unit selection can only recombine what was recorded, so a new context forces a poor join.
